title: Signs of Sine Die: Colorful hats, even more colorful barbs, a tuba, farewells and more
summary: There was still serious work to be done as the 2026 General Assembly session powered toward a midnight deadline, but in Annapolis tradition, lawmakers still found time in their 14-hour day to be not so serious.
content:
by Christine Condon, Danielle J. Brown and William J. Ford, Maryland Matters April 13, 2026

by Christine Condon, Danielle J. Brown and William J. Ford, Maryland Matters April 13, 2026

The House chamber was abuzz with Sine Die energy Monday morning. As lawmakers milled about before session began, Del. Kevin Hornberger (R-Cecil) was skatting into the microphone. When House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk (D-Prince George’s and Anne Arundel) arrived in a lacy greenish-yellow top hat, the chamber erupted in cheers.

The hat didn’t last long though. Peña-Melnyk, who said the hat was a gift from the Appropriations committee, pulled it from her head after a rousing prayer from Del. Richard Metzgar (R- Baltimore County) kicked off Monday morning’s proceedings.

“I want to thank you all for allowing me to be your speaker this session,” she said before the floor session began, “And for the supporting love, the texts, the conversations, the little gifts — everything you have done for me. I could not do this on my own.”

Del. Vaughn Stewart (D-Montgomery) continued his string of pranks on his colleagues on Sine Die, this time reprising a riff from earlier in the session, when he created a fictitious band comprised of House members.

At the time, Del. Denise Roberts (D-Prince George’s) announced a newly formed band would play an end-of-session party. Band members included House Appropriations Chair Ben Barnes (D-Anne Arundel and Prince George’s), Del. Deni Taveras (D-Prince George’s) and Del. William J. Wivell (R-Washington and Frederick). Roberts was in on the joke; the band members were not.

“We heard a few weeks ago, colleagues, that a new band had formed for the Sine Die party tonight called Third Reading,” Stewart started Monday. “But what was absolutely not a joke was we all heard the chairman of Appropriations say when asked, and I quote, ‘If you find me a tuba, I’ll play it.’”

Delegates then marched out with a tuba and handed it over to Barnes, who made good on his promise to play the instrument. “Play” might be too strong a word, but he gave a hardy “whomp” on the brass instrument to uproarious applause from the chamber.

In between business at the desk, members of the House took moments to offer thanks and farewells to members who have decided to step away from the legislature and not run for reelection this year.

House Minority Whip Jesse T. Pippy (R-Frederick) stood to give farewells to some Republican “young guns who have wised up and are moving on to brighter pastures,” pointing to Del. Joshua J. Stonko (R-Carroll) and Del. Nino Mangione (R-Baltimore).

“Josh is a young guy, very smart, very bright, has a beautiful family … and obviously he’s smart enough to keep it moving. So good for you,” Pippy said. “Nino Mangione is a fighter, he has provided a lot of contributions to our caucus…. We wish him the best and we will certainly miss him.”

Pippy then gestured over to the seat of Del. Christopher Eric Bouchat (R-Frederick and Carroll), who has received ample criticism for his ongoing absence from the House floor since late February.

“And last, but not least, I have prepared a very extensive and heartfelt speech for my friend from Carroll County. If he could rise,” Pippy asked, knowing that Bouchat would not be there to stand. Bouchat was once again not in attendance, represented only by a small figure of Socrates sitting at his desk.

“Oh, OK, never mind,” Pippy said, sitting down while other lawmakers laughed.

Farewells also took up a fair amount of floor time in the Senate, where five senators have said they will not be coming back next year.

Sen. Chris West (R-Baltimore and Carroll), a two-term senator who served a term in the House before that, was invited up to the rostrum — which he noted was still unfamiliar turf to him after 12 years.

“This is my first time up here … so I guess I’ve risen in the world,” West said from the dais.

During his slightly more than five-minute remarks — a colloquy, to use one of West’s favorite words — West said he was able to get more than 100 bills approved, “some very important, other less so, some even piffles, but all of which are making life better for the over six million citizens of Maryland.”

His last bill, Senate Bill 840, calling for a state study of the amount of electricity from certain facilities, including nuclear power, wind and solar, never got out of committee. But he also co-sponsored a successful Democratic-led bill that limits the number of offenses for which youth can be automatically charged in adult courts. West has said data shows the bill will save time for the courts, since most offenses referred to adult court ultimately revert to juvenile court.

Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City) honored West by reading back what he has said about political moderation. “Politics is the science of addition, not subtraction,” Ferguson said. “Trying to purge the party of people more conversative or more moderate than you merely wastes time, creates festering animosities and makes the accomplishment of election victories more difficult.”

Ferguson later honored Sen. Pamela Beidle (D-Anne Arundel), citing her history as a business owner, an Anne Arundel County Council member from 1998 to 2006 and a member of the House from 2007 to 2019. She joined the Senate in 2019, and has been chair of the Finance Committee since 2023.

Beidle thanked the Finance Committee and its vice chair, Sen. Antonio Hayes (D-Baltimore City), and the entire Senate. Retiring along with Beidle will be her chief of staff for her 20 years in the legislature, Nancy Crawford.

“It’s hard to give it up, but I think you know when it’s time,” Beidle said. “I will miss all of you. I’ll come back and visit … Before I ride into the sunset, I just want to thank all of you for your friendship.”
